author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction, October 1974
card_summary: In a near-future California, Congress has extended abortion law past birth: a child has no soul, and so no legal protection, until it can do algebra — a test the law sets at twelve.
page_summary:
In a near-future California, Congress has extended abortion law past birth: a child has no soul, and so no legal protection, until it can do algebra — a test the law sets at twelve. Unwanted children up to that age can be surrendered by their parents to a County Facility, collected by a white truck that plays a nursery rhyme through a loudspeaker, held thirty days for adoption, and then killed. Walter Best, who is twelve and therefore safe, hides in the brambles when the truck passes anyway; his mother explains that his fear is irrational and legally groundless, and he concludes that she is the one without a soul. The truck's driver, Ferris, picks up a boy named Tim Gantro who has no Desirability card. Tim's father Ed Gantro — a Stanford graduate in mathematics with a further degree in psychology — demands to be taken too, on the grounds that he cannot do algebra and therefore has no soul either. His argument is that the line is arbitrary and that either all of them should be killed or none. At the Facility the manager recognises the trap, discovers Gantro's qualifications, and orders him expelled before the press arrives; they arrive anyway. Ian Best, Walter's father, drives down to collect them, drunk and delighted. The story ends with the two men agreeing that they will never actually escape to Vancouver Island, and driving home in silence.

**Why it matters.** As argument, the story is a reductio: it takes a threshold theory of personhood and moves the threshold until the reader's assent breaks. Its most effective stroke is procedural rather than rhetorical — Gantro cannot be released without conceding that the criterion is arbitrary, and cannot be held without the state killing an adult, so the institution simply expels him and denies everything. As fiction, its quality is uneven in a way worth recording: Walter's chapters are observed and particular, while the Best household scenes are broad caricature, and the story's anger is distributed unevenly between the policy and the women who are made to voice it.

structure.form: novelette in five movements, alternating between the children, the truck, and the two households
movements: Walter in the brambles, and his mother's legal reassurance.
The boys in the yard, working out what could be done about the truck.
Ferris's pickup of Tim Gantro, and Ed Gantro's demand to be taken as well.
The Best household: Cynthia's enthusiasm for having an abortion, and Ian's drinking.
The Facility, the press, and the drive home.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between Walter, Ferris, Ian Best and Ed Gantro. The shifts are used to give the polemic more than one mouth.
structure.rhetorical_method: The story argues by extension: it accepts the logic that personhood begins at a legally set threshold and pushes the threshold forward until the result is monstrous. Gantro states the argument outright in the truck — that the line was always arbitrary and that the Greeks of Plato's time would have failed the algebra test.

characters.name: Walter Best
characters.role: twelve; legally safe and still frightened
characters.note: The story's best-realised figure. His reasoning — that if he has a soul now he had one two years ago, or nobody has one — is the argument stated by a child before any adult makes it.

characters.name: Ed Gantro
characters.note: Claims to have lost his soul to an embolism and to have forgotten algebra. His demand to be caged is the story's central action and its most effective device: a protest that works precisely because it cannot be refused without conceding the point.

characters.name: Tim Gantro
characters.note: Picked up for lacking a ninety-dollar Desirability card his father could not afford.

characters.name: Oscar Ferris
characters.note: Given interior monologue, and it is coarse and incurious. He defends the work in the language of population policy and says it lets him move around and meet people.

characters.name: Ian Best
characters.note: Drunk, defeated, and the source of the story's harshest rhetoric. His long speech about 'castrating females' is the passage the reception file turns on.

characters.name: Cynthia Best
characters.note: Wants an abortion because it is fashionable and one can discuss it with visitors. The story's least mediated caricature.

characters.name: Sam B. Carpenter
characters.note: Recognises Gantro as a protester and thinks entirely in terms of headlines and appropriations.

settings.name: The California coast near Big Sur
settings.note: Highway One, canyons, strays scratching about in the fields.

settings.name: The abortion truck
settings.note: Wire cages, a gas button for obstreperous passengers, a shotgun mounted across the cab, and a tape loop playing a nursery rhyme.

settings.name: The County Facility
settings.note: A green-painted building where children wait thirty days behind a fence, showing well to visitors.

motifs: The nursery rhyme played from the truck, switched off during a collection and back on afterwards
Algebra as the legal test of a soul, and Gantro's forgetting of it as his defence
Euphemism: 'put them to sleep', 'pre-person', 'child protection shelter', the Desirability card
Vancouver Island as the escape that both men know will not happen
The pound truck for dogs and cats, treated by the children as the same institution and by the adults as an obvious comparison

distinctive_terms.label: Plato
distinctive_terms.note: From Gantro's argument that the Greeks of Plato's time knew only geometry and would have failed the algebra test.

distinctive_terms.label: Church
distinctive_terms.note: The Church of Watchers, which lobbied Congress and wanted the threshold set at three.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick defended the story vigorously at the time, recorded the hostility it drew, and softened his account of his own motive by 1980.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: In this I incurred the absolute hate of Joanna Russ who wrote me the nastiest letter I've ever received; at one point she said she usually offered to beat up people (she didn't use the word "people") who expressed opinions such as this. I admit that this story amounts to special pleading, and I am sorry to offend those who disagree with me about abortion on demand. I also got some unsigned hate mail, some of it not from individuals but from organizations promoting abortion on demand. Well, I…
evidence.reading: Documents the story's real-world reception: hate mail, including a threatening letter from Joanna Russ, which the dossier's own critical_caution field should be read alongside.

evidence.source: Selected Letters — to Vonda McIntyre, 8 July 1975
evidence.quote: I received a fanzine with a piece of yours in it attacking "The Pre-Persons" as "vicious." The story was written out of a love for small &. helple…
evidence.reading: Dick answering a named fellow writer directly. His defence is about motive — love for the helpless — rather than about the story's treatment of the women in it, which was the objection.

evidence.quote: I got a lot of unsigned hate mail on that.
evidence.reading: His own account of the reception.

evidence.quote: This story runs 6,000 words and is called "The Pre-Persons," and deals with abortions (it's against, not for).
evidence.reading: Describing the commission to a correspondent. Note the word count: he gives 6,000 against a finished text of roughly 10,000, so this is likely a draft or projected length.

evidence.source: Quoted in Sutin, from Dick's 1980 Afterword
evidence.quote: In `The Pre-Persons' it is love for the children that I feel, not anger toward those …
evidence.reading: A retrospective softening. Sutin introduces it with the statement that Dick later regretted the vehemence, which makes this the closest thing to a retraction in the file.

criticism.summary: The critics treat it as the point where Dick's handling of women in his fiction became a problem in its own right.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: The high-water mark of the "problem" came in Phil's 1974 short story "The Pre-Persons," which reflects Phil's deeply felt antiabortion stand.
evidence.reading: Sutin is discussing a running 'problem' in Dick's portrayal of women and identifies this story as its extreme point.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: as if female fetuses did not exist.
evidence.reading: Sutin's sharpest formulation: the story's rhetoric is conducted entirely in terms of boys and men, which he takes as revealing about what the anger is actually directed at.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: Dick was just as emphatic about a later story, "The Pre-Persons" (1974, CS5), which is equally direct in its morality
evidence.reading: Palmer pairs it with 'Human Is', which Dick called his credo, as the two stories where he wrote directly and emphatically about morality. Elsewhere Palmer calls this one offensive and uses 'Human Is' as its inoffensive foil.

contradictions.summary: Dick defends the story's vehemence in 1975 and disowns it in 1980.

claim_a.text: written out of a love for small & helpless…, answering a charge of viciousness

claim_b.text: it is love for the children that I feel, not anger toward those…

contradictions.note: Sutin frames the 1980 statement as regret for the vehemence. Both are Dick's; the five-year gap and the change of audience are part of the evidence.

contradictions.summary: Dick says the story was written out of love; contemporary readers and later critics say its anger is directed at women.

claim_a.text: love for small and helpless things; love for the children, not anger

claim_b.text: 'vicious'; the high-water mark of the problem; as if female fetuses did not exist

contradictions.note: Kept in full. The dossier's own reading notes that the story routes its anger through its female characters, which is an observation about the text rather than an adjudication of the politics.

open_questions: Vonda McIntyre's fanzine piece calling the story 'vicious' is not in the archive. It is the primary contemporary criticism and Dick answers it directly; worth locating.
Dick's 1980 Afterword survives here only as a fragment quoted by Sutin. The full text would settle how far the retraction goes.
Dick describes the commission as a 6,000-word story against a finished text near 10,000. Is there a shorter draft in the record?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
